title: Phishing for Information
summary: Phishing for information is social engineering delivered by message, where the objective is data rather than code execution. That single difference separates it from the delivery technique that drops a payload: here the attacker wants the victim to type a password, describe an internal system, or confirm a schedule. Messages arrive by email, chat, social media, or voice, and they lean on a believable pretext plus time pressure. The telemetry sits mostly on the message side: mail gateway records, sender authentication results, the age of the sending domain, and the reply chain. A fake login page produces proxy or DNS records for a domain the organisation has no relationship with. Distinguishing this from ordinary marketing mail comes down to sender authenticity checks, domain age, and whether a request for information makes sense for the sender's role.

beginner.definition: Phishing for information means tricking a person into giving away facts. The attacker sends a message and pretends to be someone trustworthy. They may ask for a password, a system name, or a meeting time. The goal is information rather than running harmful software.
beginner.whyItMatters: One reply can hand over the details an attacker needs for a later break-in. A password or a list of internal systems is often enough. These messages use normal channels, so technical filters alone will not catch them all. People are the target, so training and a simple reporting habit matter. A fast report can also warn the rest of the company.
howItWorks: The attacker studies public information to choose a person and a believable story.
They send a message by email, chat, or social media, often with a sense of urgency.
The message asks for a small piece of information, such as a password or a process.
They may include a link to a page that copies a real login screen.
They collect what the victim sends and reply again to ask for more.
They reuse what they learn for later scanning, phishing, or access attempts.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital night desk. A caller says they are from the supplier and needs the ward door code for a delivery. The code is not a weapon, but it opens the door. The receptionist gives it because the story sounds ordinary. Phishing for information is that phone call, sent by message, repeated until it works once.
takeaways: Any request for a password or a system detail deserves a check through another channel.
Report suspicious messages quickly so that others can be warned.
Keep public information about your staff and your systems modest.

objectives: Define phishing for information and contrast it with payload phishing.
Describe the delivery channels that attackers use to reach a target.
Explain the social engineering cues that appear in these messages.
Identify the log sources that record suspicious message delivery.
Explain how a reported message becomes a useful warning for others.
